chapters.n: Nehemiah tells his own story, much like a personal journal. It is late in the year 445 BC, and he is serving in the Persian winter palace at Susa, about thirteen years after Ezra went to Jerusalem.

f.g: The ninth month (Kislev), roughly November–December.
The twentieth year of King Artaxerxes I, about 445 BC (Nehemiah 2:1).
Susa, a royal capital of Persia in what is now southwestern Iran; also the setting of Esther.

chapters.n: Visitors arrive from Judah, including Nehemiah’s brother Hanani. Though Nehemiah has a comfortable life at court, his first question is about his people and the holy city.

f.g: Those who survived the exile and returned to Judah.

chapters.n: The news is grim: the returned exiles are struggling and mocked, and Jerusalem’s walls and gates still lie in ruins. Without walls, a city was defenseless and disgraced.

f.g: Disgrace, scorn from others.

f.w: the wall of Jerusalem also is broken down

chapters.n: Nehemiah weeps, mourns, fasts, and prays for days. Before doing anything, he takes the problem to God. Four months pass before he speaks to the king (Nehemiah 2:1).
Nehemiah begins by praising God as great, awe-inspiring, and faithful to His covenant. He reminds himself whom he is speaking to before he asks for anything.

f.g: In KJV English, “inspiring awe,” not “bad.”

chapters.n: He asks God to listen, then confesses Israel’s sins — and includes himself and his own family. Like Ezra and Daniel, he does not point fingers but shares the blame.

f.g: Persistent, continuing prayer.

f.w: both I and my father's house have sinned

chapters.n: Nehemiah admits plainly that Israel failed to keep the law given through Moses.

f.g: Laws and decrees.
Rulings, legal ordinances.

chapters.n: Now he appeals to God’s own word. Moses had warned that disobedience would bring scattering — and that warning came true.

f.w: I will scatter you abroad among the nations

chapters.n: But Moses also promised that if Israel returned to the Lord, He would gather them again, even from the ends of the earth. Nehemiah is praying in faith on a promise. Latter-day Saints see this same promise being fulfilled in the gathering of Israel today.

f.w: the place that I have chosen to set my name there

chapters.n: Nehemiah reminds God that these are still His people, whom He redeemed from Egypt with His mighty hand. Redemption is a covenant word: God had bought them back as His own.

He closes with a specific request: success “this day” when he approaches the king. Only now do we learn that Nehemiah is the king’s cupbearer — a trusted official close to the most powerful man in the world.

f.g: The king, Artaxerxes — great to the world, but just “this man” before God.
The official who served and tasted the king’s wine, guarding against poison; a highly trusted adviser.

f.w: grant him mercy in the sight of

chapters.n: Four months after hearing the bad news, Nehemiah is serving wine to the king. He had always been careful to look cheerful at court, but now his sorrow shows.

f.g: The first month, roughly March–April; four months after Chisleu (Nehemiah 1:1).

f.w: I had not been beforetime sad in his presence
f.g: Showing sadness before a Persian king could be seen as disloyal and was risky.

chapters.n: The king notices immediately and recognizes it is grief, not illness. Nehemiah is terrified — this was a dangerous moment, but also the opening he had prayed for.

f.g: Face, expression.
Extremely frightened.

chapters.n: Nehemiah answers wisely. He begins with a respectful royal greeting and speaks of his ancestors’ graves rather than naming Jerusalem — something any Persian would respect.

f.w: Let the king live for ever

f.g: Tombs, graves.

chapters.n: The king asks what he wants. Before answering, Nehemiah sends up a silent prayer — a quick, heartfelt plea in the middle of a conversation.

f.w: So I prayed to the God of heaven

chapters.n: Nehemiah makes a bold, clear request: send me to rebuild the city. His months of prayer had prepared him to know exactly what to ask.
The king, with the queen beside him, asks only how long he will be gone. Nehemiah gives a time — he had already thought through the plan. He later stayed as governor for twelve years.
Nehemiah asks for letters of safe passage through the provinces west of the Euphrates. He combined faith with careful practical planning.

f.g: West of the Euphrates — the Persian province that included Judah.
Let me pass through safely.

chapters.n: He also asks for timber from the king’s forest for the temple fortress gates, the city wall, and his own residence. The king grants everything, and Nehemiah gives the credit to God.

f.w: the palace which appertained to the house
f.g: The fortress next to the temple (“the house”).

f.w: the good hand of my God upon me

chapters.n: Unlike Ezra, who chose to travel without soldiers (Ezra 8:22), Nehemiah goes with a royal military escort. Both men trusted God; each did what fit his situation.

f.w: captains of the army and horsemen

chapters.n: Two powerful neighbors are upset. Sanballat was governor of Samaria to the north; Tobiah was an Ammonite official to the east. They did not want a strong Jerusalem.

f.g: Probably from Beth-horon; an ancient papyrus from Egypt confirms a Sanballat as governor of Samaria.
“Servant” likely means a royal official; he had family ties with Jewish leaders (Nehemiah 6:17-18).

chapters.n: Nehemiah rests three days after the long journey before acting, just as Ezra did.
He inspects the walls secretly at night with a few men. He keeps his plan quiet until he understands the problem fully.

f.w: what my God had put in my heart

chapters.n: Leaving by the Valley Gate on the west side, he heads south past a spring to the Dung Gate, surveying the ruined walls.

f.g: Perhaps “jackal’s spring” or “serpent’s spring”; its exact location is uncertain.
The Dung Gate, where rubbish was carried out of the city to the Hinnom Valley.

chapters.n: Near the southeast corner, the rubble is so thick his animal cannot get through.

f.g: The Fountain Gate, near the Pool of Siloam in the south.
Possibly the Pool of Siloam or one near it, connected to Hezekiah’s water tunnel (2 Kings 20:20).

chapters.n: He goes up the Kidron Valley on the east side on foot, then turns back and returns the way he came.

f.g: The Kidron Valley, east of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: No one in the city knew what he had been doing. Nehemiah gathered the facts before sharing his vision.

f.g: Leading families of Judah.

chapters.n: Now Nehemiah speaks to the leaders. He uses “we” and “us,” joining himself with them, and appeals to their shared shame and hope.

f.w: that we be no more a reproach

chapters.n: He shares his testimony of God’s help and the king’s support. The people respond eagerly, “Let us rise up and build,” and commit themselves to the work.

f.w: Let us rise up and build

f.g: Encouraged one another; prepared themselves for the task.

chapters.n: The enemies mock and accuse the Jews of rebellion — the same charge that had stopped rebuilding before. A third opponent, Geshem, leader of Arab tribes to the south, joins them.

f.g: A powerful leader of Arab tribes; his name appears on an ancient silver bowl found in Egypt.

f.w: will ye rebel against the king?

chapters.n: Nehemiah answers firmly that God will make them succeed. The opponents have no share, no legal right, and no heritage in Jerusalem — this work belongs to God’s covenant people.

f.w: The God of heaven, he will prosper us

f.g: A rightful remembrance or historic claim.

chapters.n: The tour of the wall begins at the northeast, near the temple, and moves counterclockwise around the city. Fittingly, the high priest and priests start the work and dedicate their section to God.

f.g: Near the temple, where sheep for sacrifice were likely brought in; compare the pool by the sheep market in John 5:2.
Dedicated it to the Lord as holy.
Means “Hundred” — perhaps the Tower of the Hundred.

chapters.n: Men from Jericho, about 15 miles away, help build. People from towns all over Judah came to work on the capital’s wall.
The Fish Gate on the north side was probably where fishermen from Tyre and Galilee brought their catch to market. This family rebuilt it completely, beams to locks.

f.g: Heavy bolts placed across gates to lock them.

chapters.n: Meremoth, the priest who had received Ezra’s treasure, repairs here — and he will repair a second section later (verse 21). Some workers did double duty.
The ordinary people of Tekoa work hard, but their nobles refuse to bend their necks to the labor. It is the one sour note in the list — pride kept some from serving.

f.g: People of Tekoa, a town south of Bethlehem and home of the prophet Amos (Amos 1:1).

f.w: put not their necks to the work
f.g: Like an ox refusing the yoke — unwilling to serve.

chapters.n: Two men rebuild the “Old Gate,” probably at the northwest corner of the city.

f.g: Perhaps “the gate of the old city”; some translate it “Jeshanah Gate.”

chapters.n: Men from Gibeon and Mizpah, towns north of Jerusalem, repair the next section, up to the residence used by the provincial governor.

f.w: the throne of the governor on this side the river
f.g: Probably the official seat or quarters of the Persian governor west of the Euphrates.

chapters.n: Skilled craftsmen — a goldsmith and a perfume maker — lay down their delicate trades to do rough stonework. They restore the wall as far as the “Broad Wall.”

f.g: Perfume or ointment makers.
A thick section of wall; archaeologists have found a massive wall in Jerusalem from Hezekiah’s time often linked to it.

chapters.n: Rephaiah, governor of half of the Jerusalem district, works alongside the common people. Leaders served with their own hands.

f.w: the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem
f.g: Head of one of two administrative halves of the Jerusalem district.

chapters.n: Jedaiah repairs the stretch right in front of his own house. Working near home made sense — each family protected what it loved most.

f.g: Opposite or in front of his house.

chapters.n: These two men rebuild “the other piece,” suggesting this was their second assignment, along with the Tower of the Ovens, where bread may have been baked.

f.g: The Tower of the Ovens, perhaps near the bakers’ street (Jeremiah 37:21).

chapters.n: A district ruler named Shallum works with his daughters — a lovely detail showing that women also took part in rebuilding the wall.

f.g: The only women mentioned among the builders.

chapters.n: The people of Zanoah rebuild the Valley Gate and repair about a third of a mile of wall to the Dung Gate. The long stretch may mean this part was less damaged.

f.g: About 1,500 feet (450 meters); a cubit was about 18 inches.

chapters.n: A district ruler from Beth-haccerem rebuilds the Dung Gate, through which refuse was taken out of the city.
The Fountain Gate and the wall by the Pool of Siloam are rebuilt, near the stairs leading down from the oldest part of Jerusalem, the City of David.

f.g: The Pool of Siloam, fed by Hezekiah’s tunnel; compare John 9:7.
The original hill of Jerusalem that David captured (2 Samuel 5:7).

chapters.n: Another man named Nehemiah (not the governor) repairs the area across from King David’s tombs, near a reservoir and the old barracks of David’s warriors.

f.g: Probably barracks for the king’s elite soldiers (2 Samuel 23:8).

chapters.n: Levites join the work, along with a ruler from Keilah, a town southwest of Jerusalem.
The other half of the Keilah district is represented by its ruler, Bavai. Both halves of the district contributed.
Ezer, ruler of Mizpah, repairs a section near the armory, where the wall turns a corner.

f.g: A storehouse for weapons.

chapters.n: Baruch is the only builder described as working “earnestly” — eagerly, with fire. His section reaches the high priest’s house.

f.g: With zeal or burning energy; the only worker singled out this way.

chapters.n: Meremoth takes on his second section, the length of the high priest’s large house.
Priests from the surrounding countryside, probably the Jordan Valley region, do their share.

f.g: Men of the surrounding region, likely the Jordan Valley.

chapters.n: More men repair the wall beside their own homes. When everyone strengthens the part closest to them, the whole city becomes secure.
Binnui repairs from Azariah’s house to the corner where the wall bends.

f.g: A corner or angle where the wall changes direction.

chapters.n: This section runs past a tower projecting from the old royal palace near the prison courtyard — the area where Jeremiah was once held.

f.g: The upper palace of the former kings of Judah.

chapters.n: The temple servants lived on Ophel, the hill between the temple and the City of David, near the Water Gate on the east. The Water Gate later becomes the place where Ezra reads the law.

f.g: Means “swelling” or “hill” — the ridge just south of the temple mount.

chapters.n: The people of Tekoa do a second section, even though their nobles refused to help (verse 5). The common people made up for their leaders’ pride.
Priests repair near the Horse Gate, each one in front of his own house.
A priest and the keeper of the East Gate repair next. Each gate had its own guardians.

f.g: A gate facing east toward the Mount of Olives.

chapters.n: Meshullam repairs in front of his own room. Sadly, his family later formed a marriage alliance with Nehemiah’s enemy Tobiah.

f.g: A room or dwelling.

chapters.n: Malchiah, son of a goldsmith, works near the quarters of temple servants and merchants, close to the Inspection Gate.

f.g: Means “muster” or “inspection” — the Inspection Gate, perhaps where people or goods were counted.

chapters.n: Goldsmiths and merchants close the circle, finishing back at the Sheep Gate where the high priest began. The whole wall was rebuilt by a united people, each doing a part.
As the wall rises, so does the opposition. Sanballat’s first weapon is ridicule — mockery meant to make the builders feel foolish and give up.

f.g: Angry.
Became furious.

chapters.n: In front of Samaria’s soldiers, Sanballat fires off scornful questions: Can these weak Jews really finish? Can they bring burned stones back to life? Burned limestone often crumbles, so his taunt had a sting of truth.

f.g: Weak, withered.
Make usable again the fire-damaged stones from the Babylonian destruction.

chapters.n: Tobiah adds a joke: the wall is so flimsy a fox could knock it over. Critics often attack the worth of the work as well as the workers.

f.g: Even a light animal like a fox (or jackal) would topple it — a sarcastic insult.

chapters.n: Instead of answering the mockers, Nehemiah turns to God in prayer, asking Him to turn their insults back on them.

f.w: turn their reproach upon their own head

chapters.n: His prayer is strong, like some of the Psalms, asking God not to overlook their sin. The enemies were not just insulting builders — they were fighting against God’s work.
The result: the wall reaches half its height all the way around, because “the people had a mind to work.” Unity and willing hearts did what mockery said was impossible.

f.w: the people had a mind to work
f.g: Literally “the people had a heart to work” — they were wholehearted.
To half its full height, all around the city.

chapters.n: Now Jerusalem is surrounded by enemies on every side: Samaria in the north, Arabs in the south, Ammon in the east, and Ashdod (the old Philistine region) in the west.

f.g: People of Ashdod, a former Philistine city on the coast west of Judah.
Gaps or holes in the wall.

chapters.n: Mockery turns to a conspiracy to attack and stop the work by force.
Nehemiah’s response shows a pattern: pray, and post guards. Faith and practical action work together.

f.w: we made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch

chapters.n: Then discouragement spreads inside Judah. The workers are exhausted, the rubble seems endless, and they fear they cannot finish. In Hebrew this verse sounds like a short, sad work chant.

f.g: Those carrying away rubble and carrying in materials.
Failing, giving out.

chapters.n: Meanwhile the enemies plan a surprise attack to kill the builders and end the work.
Jews living in nearby towns come again and again to warn of attack from every direction. “Ten times” means repeatedly; fear can spread through constant rumors.

f.g: An idiom for “over and over.”

chapters.n: Nehemiah stations armed families at the lowest, weakest points behind the wall and on the high places, where enemies could see them ready. Families guarding together had every reason to stand firm.

f.g: Arranged by family groups.

chapters.n: Nehemiah encourages them: don’t fear — remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your families and homes. Remembering God is the cure for fear.

f.w: fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses

chapters.n: Once the enemies realize their plot is known, they back off. Nehemiah sees God’s hand in this, and everyone goes back to work.

f.g: Frustrated their plan, made it come to nothing.

chapters.n: From then on, half of Nehemiah’s men work while the other half stand guard in armor, with leaders backing them up.

f.g: Coats of armor, chain mail.
Worked.

chapters.n: Carriers work with one hand and hold a weapon with the other. It is a vivid picture of building God’s kingdom while staying on guard against what would destroy it.

f.g: Loaded others with burdens.

f.w: with the other hand held a weapon

chapters.n: Each builder wears a sword while working. A trumpeter stays at Nehemiah’s side, ready to sound the alarm.

f.g: Fastened at his waist.
The shofar, a ram’s horn, used to call people together or sound alarm.

chapters.n: Nehemiah explains the danger: the wall is long and workers are spread thin.

f.g: Spread out along the wall, far apart.

chapters.n: So he gives a simple plan: when you hear the trumpet, rally to it, and God will fight for us. They would face trouble together, not alone.

f.w: our God shall fight for us

chapters.n: The work went on from dawn until the stars came out, with half of the men always on guard.

f.g: Until nightfall.

chapters.n: Workers from outside towns stay in Jerusalem overnight to serve as night guards. Everyone took a share of both labor and watching.
Nehemiah and his men never changed out of their clothes, staying ready at all times. The last phrase is hard to translate; many think it means each kept his weapon at hand, even when going for water.

f.w: saving that every one put them off for washing
f.g: The Hebrew is unclear; it may mean “each kept his weapon in his right hand” or “even at the water.”

chapters.n: A new threat arises — not from outside enemies but from within. Poor families, wives included, cry out against fellow Jews who are taking advantage of them.

f.g: Fellow Israelites — making the injustice a betrayal of covenant brotherhood.

chapters.n: Large families cannot get enough grain to survive. Working on the wall may have left them less time to farm.

f.g: In KJV English, grain in general — wheat or barley, not American maize.

chapters.n: Others have mortgaged their fields, vineyards, and homes just to buy food during a famine.

f.g: Famine, scarcity.
Pledged as security for a loan.

chapters.n: Still others borrowed against their land to pay the Persian king’s taxes. Imperial taxes were heavy, and the poor were caught between taxes and lenders.

f.g: Taxes owed to the Persian king.

chapters.n: Their bitter cry: we are the same flesh and blood as the rich, yet our children are being sold into servitude to pay debts, and we can’t buy them back because others now own our land.

f.w: our flesh is as the flesh of our brethren
f.g: We are of the same family and people.
Buy back from servitude.

chapters.n: Nehemiah is angry — righteously so. Injustice toward the poor is a serious offense against God.
He first thinks it through, then confronts the leaders openly. Charging interest to fellow Israelites in need was forbidden by the law of Moses.

f.g: I thought it over carefully.
Charging interest on loans; here also taking pledges from the poor.

chapters.n: Nehemiah points out the irony: we have spent money buying back Jews sold to foreigners, and now you are selling your own brothers! The nobles have no answer.

f.g: Fell silent.

chapters.n: He appeals to their witness before the nations. Mistreating one another gives their enemies a reason to mock Israel and its God.

f.w: walk in the fear of our God
f.g: Live with reverent respect for God.

chapters.n: Nehemiah admits that he and his men also lent money and grain. He includes himself: “let us” stop this practice.

f.g: Stop, give up.

chapters.n: He calls for immediate restitution: give back the land, homes, and the interest charged. True repentance includes making things right.

f.g: Olive groves.
One percent — likely a monthly interest rate, about 12 percent a year.

chapters.n: The nobles agree. To make it binding, Nehemiah has them swear an oath before the priests.
Nehemiah shakes out the fold of his robe as a symbol: may God shake out anyone who breaks this promise. The people say “Amen,” praise the Lord, and keep their word.

f.g: Shook out the fold of his garment, which was used like a pocket — an acted-out curse.
Hebrew for “so be it” or “truly.”

chapters.n: Nehemiah now looks back over his twelve years as governor (445–433 BC). He never claimed the food allowance a governor was entitled to collect from the people.

f.g: The governor’s official food allowance, paid by taxes on the people.

chapters.n: Earlier governors had burdened the people with heavy charges, and their staff bullied the people. Nehemiah refused to, out of reverence for God.

f.g: Burdensome, demanding payment.
A shekel was a weight of silver, about 0.4 ounce (11 grams).

f.w: because of the fear of God

chapters.n: Rather than using his position to buy up land cheaply from struggling families, Nehemiah and his servants worked on the wall.

f.g: He did not profit from others’ hardship.

chapters.n: He fed 150 officials daily at his own table, plus visitors from other nations — paying from his own resources.

f.g: Governors were expected to host officials and guests.

chapters.n: His daily menu was large, yet he still didn’t demand the governor’s allowance, because the people were already weighed down. Leaders who serve without burdening others follow a higher pattern.

f.w: the bondage was heavy upon this people
store of all sorts of wine
f.g: An abundant supply of wine.

chapters.n: Nehemiah ends with a short prayer, one of several in his memoir: remember me for good. He looks to God, not to people, for his reward.

f.w: Think upon me, my God, for good

chapters.n: The wall is nearly done — every gap closed, though the gate doors are not yet hung. With mockery and threats failing, the enemies change tactics again.

f.g: No gaps remaining in the wall.

chapters.n: Sanballat and Geshem invite Nehemiah to a “friendly” meeting in the plain of Ono, about 25 miles away near the coast. It was a trap to harm him.

f.g: A valley northwest of Jerusalem near modern Tel Aviv, on the edge of Judah’s territory.
Harm, evil.

chapters.n: Nehemiah’s famous answer: I am doing a great work and cannot come down. He refuses to be distracted from what God has asked him to do.

f.w: I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down

chapters.n: They ask four times; he gives the same answer four times. Persistence in temptation is met with persistence in purpose.
The fifth message is an unsealed letter — meant to be read by others along the way and to spread the rumor.

f.g: An unsealed letter, so its accusations would become public gossip.

chapters.n: The letter claims Nehemiah is building the wall to rebel and make himself king. This was a dangerous charge in the Persian Empire and had stopped the work once before.

f.g: Another form of the name Geshem.

chapters.n: It even claims he has hired prophets to proclaim him king. The threat is clear: meet with us, or we will report this to Artaxerxes.

f.w: There is a king in Judah
f.g: Hopes for a restored Davidic king were real, which made the rumor believable.

chapters.n: Nehemiah flatly denies it: you made this up. He doesn’t waste time defending himself at length.

f.w: thou feignest them out of thine own heart
f.g: You are inventing these things yourself.

chapters.n: Nehemiah sees the real goal: to frighten the builders so they would quit. His response is a short prayer — “O God, strengthen my hands.”
Now a fellow Jew, Shemaiah, who claims to have a prophecy, urges Nehemiah to hide inside the temple because assassins are coming.

f.g: Confined to his house — perhaps pretending to be in danger, or in a ritual state.
The holy place, where only priests were allowed (Numbers 18:7).

chapters.n: Nehemiah refuses. A leader running to hide would discourage the people, and as a layman he had no right to enter the temple’s holy place.

f.w: Should such a man as I flee?
f.g: A governor fleeing would shatter the people’s courage.

chapters.n: Nehemiah discerns that this “prophecy” was not from God — Shemaiah had been bribed by the enemies. Spiritual discernment protected him.
The plan was to scare Nehemiah into sinning so he would lose credibility. Enemies often try to destroy a leader’s reputation when they can’t stop the work.

f.g: Grounds for slander.

chapters.n: Nehemiah again leaves justice to God. He names a false prophetess, Noadiah, and others who joined the scheme to frighten him.

f.g: Mentioned only here; one of several false prophets working against Nehemiah.

chapters.n: The wall is finished in only fifty-two days — an astonishing speed, achieved through unity, hard work, and God’s help.

f.g: The sixth month, roughly August–September, 445 BC.
About seven and a half weeks.

chapters.n: The surrounding nations lose heart, recognizing that this work was done with God’s help. The finished wall became a witness of God’s power.

f.w: cast down in their own eyes
f.g: Lost their confidence; were humbled.

f.w: this work was wrought of our God

chapters.n: An inside problem remains: some nobles of Judah were secretly in steady contact with Tobiah.
Tobiah had married into a leading Jewish family, and his son married the daughter of Meshullam, one of the wall’s builders. These marriage ties gave him loyal allies inside Jerusalem.

f.g: Bound to him by oath or alliance.

chapters.n: These nobles praised Tobiah to Nehemiah and passed Nehemiah’s words back to Tobiah, while Tobiah kept sending threatening letters. Divided loyalties among God’s people can be as dangerous as outside enemies.

f.g: Reported what I said to him — acting as informants.

chapters.n: With the wall finished and the doors hung, Nehemiah organizes the people who will guard and serve. Gatekeepers, singers, and Levites take their posts.

f.g: Gatekeepers.

chapters.n: He puts two trustworthy men in charge of the city, including his brother Hanani. Hananiah is chosen because he was faithful and reverenced God more than most.

f.g: Commander of the citadel, the fortress beside the temple (Nehemiah 2:8).
Revered God more than most men.

chapters.n: Practical security rules: keep the gates closed until well into the morning, lock them while guards are present, and post residents as watchmen, each near his own home.

f.g: Until mid-morning, when everyone is awake and alert.

chapters.n: Jerusalem was spacious, but few people lived there and many houses were still in ruins. A wall alone does not make a city — it needs people. This sets up Nehemiah 11.
God inspires Nehemiah to register the people by family. He finds the old list of the first returnees from about ninety years earlier, which he copies next.

f.w: my God put into mine heart

chapters.n: The list that follows (verses 6–73) is nearly identical to Ezra 2. It records those who returned from Babylon to their family towns.
Twelve leaders are named here (Ezra 2:2 lists eleven), perhaps symbolizing the twelve tribes. This Nehemiah and Mordecai are different men from the governor and from Esther’s cousin.

f.g: The high priest of the first return, also called Joshua (Haggai 1:1).

chapters.n: The lay families begin. Parosh was the largest clan. Small differences in numbers between this list and Ezra 2 likely come from copying errors over time or from different stages of the count.
Shephatiah’s descendants, 372 — the same number given in Ezra 2.
The family of Arah. Here the number is noticeably lower than in Ezra’s list (775).
Pahath-moab’s large clan included two branches, descended from Jeshua and Joab.

f.g: Means “governor of Moab,” perhaps recalling an ancestor’s office.

chapters.n: The family of Elam, a name shared with a land east of Babylon.
Zattu’s descendants are counted. Ezra’s list gives 945, a hundred more — an easy mix-up for scribes copying numbers.
Zaccai’s family, 760, the same as in Ezra.

f.g: Related to the name Zacchaeus (Luke 19:2), meaning “pure.”

chapters.n: Binnui’s family; Ezra 2:10 calls him Bani.

f.g: Called Bani in Ezra 2:10.

chapters.n: The family of Bebai, some of whose members later came with Ezra (Ezra 8:11).
Azgad’s family appears here with over two thousand — far more than Ezra 2:12 gives (1,222). One list may record a later stage.

f.g: Means “Gad (fortune) is strong.”

chapters.n: Descendants of Adonikam, whose name means “my Lord has risen.”

f.g: Means “my Lord has arisen.”

chapters.n: Bigvai’s large family — a Persian-sounding name, showing how exiles adopted names from their surroundings.

f.g: A Persian name; a different Bigvai was governor of Judah later in the Persian period.

chapters.n: The family of Adin, with notably more here than in Ezra’s list (454).
Ater’s family, traced through a line called Hezekiah.

f.g: The family of Ater through his descendant Hezekiah.

chapters.n: The towns of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem, including Bethel where Jacob saw the heavenly ladder.
Anathoth was Jeremiah’s hometown; Nob was the priests’ town where David once received holy bread.
Ramah, a hometown of the prophet Samuel, is among these Benjamite towns.
Three smaller towns of Benjamin.

f.g: A Benjamite town, different from the city destroyed with Sodom (Genesis 14:2).

chapters.n: Lod and Ono lay in a valley known for its craftsmen.
Some groups of Levites lived in Judah and some in Benjamin, serving among the people wherever they lived.

f.g: Groups or courses of Levites.

chapters.n: Before describing the wall’s dedication, Nehemiah lists the priestly families from the first return about ninety years earlier under Zerubbabel and Jeshua. The “Ezra” here is an earlier priest, not Ezra the scribe.

f.g: An earlier priest of the same name, from the first return around 538 BC.

chapters.n: Three more heads of priestly houses from that first generation.
Shechaniah, Rehum, and Meremoth — names that reappear in later generations of the same families.

f.g: Called Meraioth in verse 15.

chapters.n: Iddo’s priestly family later produced the prophet Zechariah, who encouraged the rebuilding of the temple.
Bilgah was one of the twenty-four priestly divisions organized by David.
Joiarib and Jedaiah were also ancient priestly divisions — Joiarib (Jehoiarib) was the first.
The list of 22 priestly leaders in Jeshua’s time closes.

f.g: Jeshua was high priest at the first return, about 538–515 BC.

chapters.n: The leading Levites of that first return, including Mattaniah, who led the songs of thanksgiving.

f.g: In charge of the thanksgiving songs.

chapters.n: Other Levites stood opposite them — the choir sang in alternating, call-and-response groups.

f.w: over against them in the watches
f.g: Facing them in their shifts — antiphonal singing, one group answering another.

chapters.n: A list of high priests from Jeshua forward. Eliashib was high priest in Nehemiah’s own day.
The line continues to Jaddua, who many think served around the end of the Persian period. This shows the list was updated after Nehemiah’s time.

f.g: Probably the same as Johanan in verses 22–23.

chapters.n: Now the next generation: heads of the priestly families under the high priest Joiakim. Each line gives the family name, then its current head.

f.g: Son of Jeshua; high priest roughly in the early 400s BC.

chapters.n: The family of the earlier priest Ezra was now led by Meshullam.
“Melicu” is likely the same family as Malluch in verse 2 — spellings varied over time.

f.g: Probably the same as Malluch (verse 2).

chapters.n: Harim’s family, led by Adna, and Meraioth’s, led by Helkai.

f.g: Corresponds to Rehum in verse 3.

chapters.n: Iddo’s family was led by Zechariah — very likely the prophet Zechariah himself.
Abijah’s house was led by Zichri. No head is named for Miniamin’s family, perhaps lost in copying.

f.g: No leader’s name follows here; it may have dropped out of the text.

chapters.n: Bilgah’s and Shemaiah’s families and their leaders.
Joiarib’s and Jedaiah’s families. Joiarib’s line was later the family of the Maccabees, who led the Jewish revolt in the 160s BC.

f.g: Ancestor of the priestly Hasmonean (Maccabean) family.

chapters.n: Sallai (Sallu) and Amok’s families and their heads.

f.g: Same as Sallu in verse 7.

chapters.n: The last two priestly families of the list.

f.g: Means “given by God.”

chapters.n: Levite and priest family heads were recorded through several high priests down to the reign of a Persian king named Darius.

f.g: Probably Darius II (423–404 BC) or Darius III (336–330 BC); scholars differ.

chapters.n: The official records of Levite families were kept in a book of chronicles — an archive of the temple, not our book of Chronicles.

f.g: An official record book, probably temple archives.

chapters.n: The Levite leaders sang praises in two choirs facing each other, following the pattern David had set up for temple worship.

f.g: Group facing group — choirs responding to each other.

f.w: the commandment of David the man of God

chapters.n: Gatekeepers guarded the storerooms at the temple gates.

f.g: Standing guard.
Storehouses at the gates.

chapters.n: These leaders served during the time of Joiakim, Nehemiah, and Ezra — the generation of restoration.

f.w: Nehemiah the governor, and of Ezra the priest, the scribe

chapters.n: Now the great celebration! Levites from all over were brought in to dedicate the wall with joyful music. Dedication turned a construction project into an offering to God.

f.g: Hebrew hanukkah — a consecration or setting apart for God.
Stringed instruments, like a lyre or small harp.

chapters.n: Singers gathered from villages around Jerusalem, including Netophah near Bethlehem.

f.g: The Netophathites, people of Netophah near Bethlehem (1 Chronicles 9:16).

chapters.n: Singers had built their own villages near Jerusalem so they could serve at the temple.
Before the celebration, the priests and Levites purified themselves, the people, the gates, and the wall. Holiness had to be prepared for, perhaps by washing and sacrifices.
Nehemiah leads the leaders up onto the wall and forms two great choirs. The first marches south (to the right) toward the Dung Gate.

f.g: Two processions or choirs.

chapters.n: Half of Judah’s leaders follow the first choir, led by Hoshaiah.

f.w: half of the princes of Judah

chapters.n: Ezra himself walks with this first group, leading it (verse 36).
More marchers. “Judah and Benjamin” may be individual men’s names or representatives of the two tribes.

f.g: Either personal names or representatives of the two tribes.

chapters.n: Priests with trumpets join the procession, led by Zechariah, a descendant of David’s musician Asaph.
Other musicians follow, playing instruments of the kind David had introduced, and Ezra the scribe leads the way. Worship was joyful and ordered.
The first choir climbs the stairs of the City of David past David’s old palace to the Water Gate on the east.
The second choir goes the opposite way, north, with Nehemiah following, past the Tower of the Ovens and the Broad Wall.
This group passes the northern gates and towers — places rebuilt in chapter 3 — and halts at the Gate of the Guard near the temple.

f.g: The Gate of the Guard, near the temple.

chapters.n: Both choirs meet at the temple, completing a circle around the city. The whole wall had been encircled with praise.
Priests with trumpets stand with Nehemiah’s group.

f.g: Means “God raises up.”

chapters.n: More priests and singers join, and the choir sings loudly under its director Jezrahiah.
Sacrifices are offered and everyone — men, women, and children — rejoices. The joy of Jerusalem could be heard far away. This was joy God Himself had given them.

f.w: God had made them rejoice with great joy

chapters.n: Officials were appointed over the storerooms to collect offerings and tithes for the priests and Levites. The people were happy to support those who served.

f.g: The shares the law of Moses assigned to priests and Levites.

chapters.n: Singers and gatekeepers performed their duties and purification rites as David and Solomon had established.

f.g: Duties of keeping the temple ritually clean.

chapters.n: Nehemiah connects their worship to the ancient pattern from David and Asaph’s day. Restoring old patterns of worship was part of restoring the covenant.

From Zerubbabel’s day to Nehemiah’s, Israel supported the singers and gatekeepers daily and gave the holy offerings to the Levites, who passed a portion to the priests. The chapter ends on a note of faithful giving — which will soon be tested.

f.g: Set apart offerings as holy.
The priests, descendants of Aaron.

chapters.n: During a public reading of the law, the people find a command that Ammonites and Moabites may not join the assembly of Israel. This chapter may describe events some years after the wall’s dedication.

f.w: in the audience of the people
f.g: In the hearing of the people.

f.w: should not come into the congregation of God for ever

chapters.n: The reason: centuries earlier these nations refused Israel food and water and hired the prophet Balaam to curse them. But God turned the curse into a blessing.

f.w: turned the curse into a blessing

chapters.n: The people separate from those of foreign descent who had mixed in without committing to the covenant. Notably, Ruth the Moabite was welcomed long before because she fully embraced Israel’s God (Ruth 1:16).
A scandal: Eliashib, the priest in charge of the temple storerooms, had formed an alliance with Tobiah — Nehemiah’s old Ammonite enemy.

f.g: Related by marriage or bound by alliance (compare Nehemiah 6:18).

chapters.n: He gave Tobiah a large room in the temple courts — a storeroom meant for offerings and tithes that supported the Levites and priests. An enemy of God’s work now had an apartment in God’s house.

f.g: Grain offerings; “meat” means food.
A fragrant resin burned as incense.

chapters.n: This happened while Nehemiah was away. After twelve years as governor, he returned to the Persian king’s court in 433 BC, then later got permission to come back.

f.g: Persian kings also held the title “king of Babylon.”

chapters.n: Back in Jerusalem, Nehemiah learns what Eliashib had done for Tobiah.

f.g: Learned of the wrong.

chapters.n: Deeply upset, Nehemiah throws all of Tobiah’s furniture out of the room — a dramatic act of cleansing the temple, a little like Jesus driving out the moneychangers.

f.w: I cast forth all the household stuff

chapters.n: He orders the rooms purified and restores the sacred vessels and offerings to their proper place.
The Levites and singers had not been receiving their share of tithes, so they had left temple service to go farm their own fields to survive.

f.g: Their assigned share of tithes and offerings.

f.w: fled every one to his field

chapters.n: Nehemiah confronts the leaders: “Why is the house of God forsaken?” — echoing their own covenant promise not to forsake it. He brings the Levites back to their posts.

f.w: Why is the house of God forsaken?

f.g: Argued, rebuked.

chapters.n: The people resume paying tithes of grain, wine, and oil. Faithful tithing kept temple service running.
He appoints a trustworthy committee — a priest, a scribe, a Levite, and an assistant — to manage the storehouses and distribute fairly. Faithfulness was the main qualification.
Nehemiah prays again: remember my good deeds for your house. His short prayers show a man who constantly worked with God in mind.

f.w: wipe not out my good deeds

chapters.n: Nehemiah sees people working and trading on the Sabbath — pressing grapes, loading donkeys, and bringing goods to sell in Jerusalem. He warns them.

f.g: Crushing grapes by foot — farm labor forbidden on the Sabbath.
Loading.

chapters.n: Merchants from Tyre, a Phoenician port city, were selling fish and goods to Jews on the Sabbath.

f.g: Phoenician traders from the coast of what is now Lebanon.

chapters.n: Nehemiah rebukes the nobles, who were responsible for allowing it: Why are you making the Sabbath unholy?

f.g: To treat something holy as ordinary.

chapters.n: He reminds them that Sabbath-breaking was one reason their ancestors suffered exile. Repeating the sin would bring more trouble.
Nehemiah takes practical action: the gates close at sunset Friday as the Sabbath begins and stay shut until it ends, with guards to stop any goods coming in.

f.w: began to be dark before the sabbath
f.g: The Sabbath began at sunset on Friday evening.

chapters.n: Some merchants camp outside the walls once or twice, hoping to tempt buyers to come out.

f.g: Camped outside the city.

chapters.n: Nehemiah warns them sternly that he will use force if they come again. They stop coming. Firm leadership protected the Sabbath.

f.w: I will lay hands on you
f.g: I will arrest you or use force.

chapters.n: He assigns purified Levites to guard the gates and keep the day holy, then prays for mercy. Nehemiah asks not just for reward but for God’s mercy — he knows he needs it too.

f.w: spare me according to the greatness of thy mercy

chapters.n: Another old problem returns: Jewish men marrying women from Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab — breaking the covenant they had signed.

f.w: married wives of Ashdod, of Ammon, and of Moab

chapters.n: Half their children can’t even speak Hebrew. Losing the language meant losing access to the scriptures and to Israel’s identity — a concern similar to Lehi’s reason for obtaining the brass plates.

f.w: could not speak in the Jews' language
f.g: They spoke the language of their mothers’ peoples, not Hebrew.

chapters.n: Nehemiah reacts with fierce anger — rebuking, striking some, and pulling out their hair as a sign of public disgrace — and makes them swear not to arrange such marriages. His methods reflect his time and his passion for the covenant.

f.g: A humiliating public punishment; compare Ezra, who pulled out his own hair in grief (Ezra 9:3).

chapters.n: He points to Solomon: no king was greater or more loved by God, yet his foreign wives turned his heart to idols. If Solomon could fall, so could they.

f.w: Did not Solomon king of Israel sin by these things?

f.g: Foreign women.

chapters.n: Should the rest of us follow your example and betray God too? Nehemiah frames it as a matter of loyalty to the covenant.

f.g: Foreign wives who did not worship Israel’s God.

chapters.n: Worst of all, a grandson of the high priest had married the daughter of Sanballat, Nehemiah’s chief enemy. Nehemiah drives him away.

f.g: Expelled him from Jerusalem and from priestly service.

chapters.n: Nehemiah asks God to remember those who defiled the priesthood and the sacred covenant tied to it.
He purifies the community from foreign religious influence and reorganizes the priests and Levites so each has a clear assignment.

f.g: Duties, shifts of service.

chapters.n: He arranges for the firewood and firstfruit offerings to be brought on schedule. The book ends with his simple, repeated prayer: “Remember me, O my God, for good.” Nehemiah’s legacy is faithful, persistent effort for the Lord’s house.

f.w: Remember me, O my God, for good
